coherence.reasons: Both run a clean diagnosis-to-levers-to-sequencing hierarchy, with summaries that match the slides. X's governing thought ("get close to 3.0%") honestly matches its 2.97% result. But X has internal tensions. It calls ValuMart traffic the largest risk and says "defend where ValuMart competes", yet sizes promotions as a full chain-wide rollback to 24% with zero volume loss. It argues fewer hours raise shrink, yet needs 3.8% fewer hours per sales dollar to absorb the wage rise, taken from the same Q4 stores that are also donating hours. It also labels the decline a "$35.4M shortfall" when operating income fell $32.6M. Y's base-versus-full split, headwinds inside the bridge, and promotion sizing with a volume-loss assumption and ValuMart guardrail make its claims and numbers line up more consistently. Y's slide 3 substitutes its own kick-off hypothesis, which is slightly awkward but logically coherent.

judgment.reasons: Both land on the answer key's preferred type of plan (R1, with a targeted-labor element in Y). Y weighs alternatives better: a four-option table (management plan, defend on price, margin-led plan, exit delivery as a sized fallback) and an explicit case for deferring the three long-lease exits on their 3.4–4.1 year payback. Y puts the 2027 wage step and delivery-rate rise inside the plan arithmetic, separates six data-backed levers (2.5%) from three negotiated ones (3.0%), budgets $20.5M of one-time cost with a reserve, and pre-agrees contingency levers. X's headline 2.97% leaves the wage rise out of the base (its own sensitivity shows 2.49% if not absorbed) and assumes no volume loss from the promotion reset. It budgets only $7.5M of one-time cost with no implementation spend, and dismisses exiting delivery simply as out of scope. X's plan is defensible but more fragile and less candidly traded off.

evidence.reasons: Both get the critical numbers right: margin path, promotions −$10.5M, shrink −0.5 pp, labor about 13%, e-commerce drag −$10.4M, −$12.34 per delivered order, store exits $6.6M, and a rebuttal of the 6.1% claim that includes the $8.3M net delivery cost. Both also quantify why the category team's comps evidence falls short. X states the dollar bridge and the $29.8M gap explicitly and invents fewer numbers. Y expresses the bridge in margin points and leaves the gap to FY2025 sales implicit. Y adds more team estimates: about $13M of one-time costs, a ~$88M vendor pool, a fresh-waste program worth 0.15 pt, and in-year capture rates. These are flagged, but they are not pack-supported. Against that, Y uses more of the pack: a wage/productivity decomposition, the fulfillment model reconciled in all three years, break-even fee and cannibalisation thresholds, and the 2027 wage step and 3% delivery-rate rise in the numbers. It treats the shrink–hours link as a half-to-full range rather than a single upper bound and sizes promotion volume loss. X's zero-volume-loss promotion gain and mislabelled $35.4M shortfall are weaker inferences. Net slight edge to Y.

revision.reasons: Both correctly revise management's wage-inflation hypothesis with a quantified bridge, show that falling hours absorbed most of the wage rise, size the shrink give-back of the 8% cut, and reject the plan as written. Y goes somewhat further. It runs management's plan through the same model for both the covenant and FY2028, including the wage step. It keeps what is valid in the hypothesis: labor still needs targeted action (−3% hours in Q3–Q4 stores), and the freeze is retained for home delivery only. It also tests and partly revises its own "margin fixes alone" hypothesis (only 1.8%). X rejects the hypothesis cleanly and replaces the cut with moving hours, but treats the wage headwind as something to be absorbed outside the plan numbers and does not address the freeze component beyond noting the loss persists.

overall.reasons: Both documents meet the answer key's defensibility criteria: a quantified bridge, levers sized to roughly 3.0%, and second-order effects acknowledged. Y would serve the CEO and board better. Its plan includes the known headwinds and separates evidence-backed from negotiated levers. It allocates the $25M envelope, builds a more robust FY2026 covenant bridge, weighs four options, and gives clear decision requests with contingencies and risk triggers. X is accurate and well argued on diagnosis, with slightly cleaner dollar figures. But its headline 2.97% depends on a no-volume-loss promotion rollback and an unbooked wage absorption, which makes it less reliable as a board plan.
